### Whitney Winters


### VP, Commercial and Business Development

# Don’t Auto-select Your Auto Injector: How Patient Controlled Devices Can Address The Patient Challenges of Self-Injection


**As the burden of chronic and autoimmune diseases rises, there are many promising new therapies under research on the horizon to address these diseases. Many of these novel therapies require the patient to self-inject, which can sometimes present challenges, including discomfort, anxiety, inconvenience, and a higher likelihood of not following their treatment as prescribed.\[1\]**


Pharmaceutical companies who are developing these new treatments must decide how best to deliver these medicines to patients, ensuring their selected devices are easy to use as well as efficient and effective in delivering their medicines successfully. While autoinjectors can be an obvious choice, choosing a patient-controlled device, like the SelfDose® patient-controlled injector, could address these patient challenges and, in doing so, differentiate a product in the market.


One of the most significant challenges for patients is being able to self-inject easily, which requires hand strength. Hand function declines noticeably with age, especially after 65, due to degenerative changes in the muscles, joints, nerves, and blood vessels. These natural changes, combined with common age‑related conditions like osteoporosis, arthritis, and Parkinson’s disease, further contribute to reduced strength, coordination, and overall hand ability in older adults.\[2\]. In fact, the very conditions that are causing poor hand strength may also be the reason a patient needs to self-inject in the first place, as many of these same conditions can be treated with self-injected therapies.


As manufacturers determine what may be the best device to deliver an injectable medicine to a patient in a home setting, they should consider that many aging patients may not have the full functioning of their hands and, therefore, a device that is ergonomically designed for optimal patient administration like the SelfDose injector may be the best option.


In a study published in the American Medical Journal, the benefits and challenges associated with self-injecting a treatment for rheumatoid arthritis delivered in a SelfDose injector were examined. The authors concluded that patients benefited from “the ease and simplicity of use” of the device, which enabled “confidence in the device and good adherence.” The authors also reported that the design of the SelfDose injector “enabled patients with poorer hand grip to hold the device without difficulty and administer the injection effectively with the base of their hands.” These findings were consistent with the majority of patients in the study reporting satisfaction with the device.\[3\]


The conclusions of this study are consistent with the extensive human factor data that we have collected on the SelfDose injector, which is designed differently than an autoinjector. The biggest difference is that it is not dependent on the spring-driven force of an autoinjector. Patients manually control the SelfDose injector by simply pressing it down with their palm. This means that as patients age and symptoms progress, they can still comfortably self-administer their medication.


For pharmaceutical companies looking at devices that will help them address patient challenges that exist for an aging population, the SelfDose injector is a device they should consider. The device can handle a variety of volumes, viscosities, and prefilled syringe types, and it is an off-the-shelf option that can be customized easily to a variety of manufacturing environments. Self injection does not always need to be via an autoinjector, especially when the SelfDose injector offers so many patient-friendly design options that could set a product apart in the market and lead to patient satisfaction with treatment.
